results.title: From the Return to Labriola to the Anti-Croce: Philosophy, Praxis and Human Nature in Gramsci’s Prison Notebooks
From Marx to Gramsci, from Gramsci to Marx: Historical Materialism and the Philosophy of Praxis
Bruno Widmar interprete di Antonio Labriola. L'Introduzione alle Lettere
Italian Marxism and Russian Socialism : Labriola, Gramsci and Philosophical and Cultural Questions of Revolutionary Movement (1890–1937)
results.abstract: The aim of this paper is to discuss and analyze the relationship between Italian Marxist thinkers Antonio Labriola and Antonio Gramsci on the one side and prominent representatives of the Russian Socialist and Communist movement on the other: Georgiy Plekhanov, Vladimir Lenin, and Leon Trotsky. In the history of the Socialist (and Anarchic) movement in Italy and in Russia from the end of 19th to the beginning of 20th century, there are many reasons for a more careful study of the points of contact and coincidence between two countries: first of all, because of the existence of the Italian Socialist Party influential leaders of Russian origin, such as Anna Kulisheva (known in Italy as Anna Kuliscioff) and Angelica Balabanova (Angelica Balabanoff). Italian philosopher Antonio Labriola was a significant moral and theoretical authority in the intellectual formation of the Russian socialistic democrats abroad. The influence of Labriola on the European labor movement and on the debate on historical materialism was enormous, and his rejection of the positivism and reformism in the Italian Socialist Party also had an influence on the discussions in the European socialist parties. Antonio Gramsci, the founder of the Italian Communist Party, assimilated the concept of praxis theory, as well as the rejection of positivism and the reformism of Italian socialism from Labriola; Gramsci’s idea of the creative power of the working class in the revolutionary process derives from Labriola’s arguments about classes in historical materialism. Gramsci’s interest in Labriola is associated not only with the role of the philosopher in the creation of the theory of praxis, or his teaching on historical materialism, but also with his influence on Russian Marxism.

results.title: GENTILE AND THE „MARXISMUSSTREIT" IN ITALIAN PHILOSOPHY
Revisiting Marxism in José Carlos Mariátegui
results.abstract: Ebb and Socialist for the Twenty-first Century (2014), takes us on a tour of Peru at the beginning of the twentieth century through the mind and actions of José Carlos Mariátegui. In its 10 chapters, In the Red Corner: The Marxism of José Carlos Mariátegui delves into the life of a Latin American who is considered one of the most original and innovative Marxists in the region and the world. Mariátegui was an organic intellectual who found congruence and coherence in a Gramscian (1981) philosophy of praxis of which the journal Amauta and the Frente Popular (Popular Front) were clear examples. Despite the complexity of the events of Mariátegui’s life, Gonzales details them simply, beginning with his early years in Peru and continuing with his tour of Europe and finally his return. The book introduces the Anglophone reader to the importance of the little-known Mariátegui, exploring his ideas and his life and showing the genius with which he read and interpreted the work of intellectuals such as Karl Marx, Georges Sorel, Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, Antonio Labriola, Vladimir Lenin, and Leon Trotsky, among others.

results.title: Dalla traduzione alla traducibilità: uno strumento di emancipazione teorica
Radical historicism in the Russian intellectual context
results.abstract:
This article attempts to thematize a certain trend in Russian reflection on history that manifested itself at various times throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries (although it did not become a stable intellectual tradition), which is defined here as “radical historicism.” This concept is borrowed from the Anglo-American philosopher Mark Bevir, who proposes to distinguish between two main types of historicism:
 developmental
 , which assumes a deterministic view of the historical process and its unidirectional perspective, and
 radical
 , which arose during the critical rethinking of developmental historicism that occurred in the years after the First World War. Radical historicism refuses to perceive the present as the result or logical stage of previous development and considers its
 contingent
 temporal configuration with an open ending. Ignoring the difference between the present and the past as between what exists and what does not, radical historicists prefer to talk about the difference between possibilities that have already been realized and those that have not yet been realized. In the Russian intellectual context, developmental historicism became predominant, especially thanks to the works of Georgy Plekhanov and Joseph Stalin, who laid the foundations of Soviet historical materialism. However, an alternative type of historical thinking, examples of which can be found in the works of the theorists of populist socialism Alexander Herzen, Pyotr Lavrov, and Nikolai Mikhailovsky, was not completely supplanted, but has reemerged thanks to the activities of Mikhail Gefter, whose legacy has attracted considerable interest in Russia in recent years. The article proposes methodological approaches that could help assess Gefter’s significance as an original theorist of history. Particular attention is drawn to Gefter’s interest in history as a kind of practical thinking. This interest can be explained by the influence of Antonio Gramsci, whom Gefter often refers to in his works. The connection with Gramsci and Gefter’s constant interest in Herzen helps to see his thought against the backdrop of an old tradition, which partly goes back to left-wing Hegelianism and partly to the Italian philosophy of praxis, and that can be defined as the philosophy of (historical) action (
 Die Philosophie der Tat
 ,
 Filosofia della Praxis
 ).
